title: Atlantium – Chemical-Free Ultraviolet Water Disinfection

trailer.text: Atlantium is an Israeli water technology company, established in 2003 and based in Beit Shemesh.
In 2005, Israel21c described it as an Israeli start-up that had developed the Rayo System, which disinfects water without touching it, with light that bounces inside a pipe.
According to the article, the system produces no by-products and uses very little electricity.
Its systems have been installed at Tnuva, at dairies in the US and in village drinking water systems.
In 2013 the company announced that its system had received verification from the US Environmental Protection Agency.

glance.value: US, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Australia

paragraphs.text: According to Israel21c, disinfecting water with chemicals is far from ideal.
It has by-products, and it may leave residues in the water.
According to Atlantium's brochure, chemical disinfection may produce carcinogenic by-products.
This is also a problem in agriculture.
According to the Farmers Federation, the common method is chlorination, and it is considered, among other things, outdated, wasteful and dangerous to health.
According to the Federation, chlorine in contact with water produces new compounds as side effects.
According to the article, in existing UV disinfection systems the light source is often located in the water itself, and the mercury used to generate the UV light could be dangerous if it leaks.
According to the ATS, 771 million people live without access to clean water.

stations.title: A small company in Beit Shemesh

paragraphs.text: Atlantium was established in 2003 and is based in Beit Shemesh.
It was headed by David Waxman, the CEO.
The company is located in the Har Tuv Industrial Park.
Its most prominent investor was Morris Kahn, founder of the Israeli software company Amdocs.
According to CB Insights, its investors also include Pitango and Elron Ventures.
One of the company's leaders is its CTO, Ytzhak Rozenberg, a Technion graduate.

stations.title: Light that bounces inside a pipe

paragraphs.text: In Atlantium's system, the water flows through a special pipe.
The ultraviolet light source is at the end of the pipe, behind a quartz window.
Light that is not absorbed keeps bouncing off the walls of the pipe.
It disinfects more water, up to 150 centimeters from the light source.
According to the company, the technology uses principles of fiber optics, hydraulics and light recycling to disinfect better with much less energy.
According to the ATS, the company combined old technology of a Nobel laureate with new findings.
According to the ATS, the technology is protected by more than 60 patents and ensures that the light reaches every drop of water.

According to the article in Israel21c, Atlantium prides itself that while existing methods reduce the amount of bacteria by three orders of magnitude, it reduces the level by five orders of magnitude, from 100,000 bacteria to one.

stations.title: From Tnuva to dairies in the US

paragraphs.text: In 2005, three Rayo systems were installed at Tnuva, Israel's largest dairy.
Each of them disinfects one hundred cubic meters of water per hour.
Another system was installed at a fish farm in Turkey, to keep the fish free of disease.
According to Waxman, beverage companies wanted to stop using chemicals.
They wanted greener disinfection, which also improves taste and shelf life.
In October 2009 the FDA published the new pasteurization regulations, and they paved the way for ultraviolet water disinfection at dairies in the US.
One day later, Atlantium announced its systems for the American dairy industry.

According to Yoni Glickman, CEO of Atlantium in 2009, the 2009 PMO opens the way for American dairy processors to replace heat pasteurization of water with energy-efficient, chemical-free UV technology.
Tim Griglack of United Dairy said that the system had a great impact on efficiency and quality at the plant.
According to Mark Doray of Galliker's dairy, pasteurized-equivalent water is always available to them on demand.
In 2005 Atlantium planned to demonstrate in the US that the system could disinfect city drinking water.
Until then, EPA rules had established that ultraviolet light could not be used to meet the high virus threshold, which was set according to adenovirus.
According to Phyllis Posy of the company, many water suppliers and regulators hesitated to switch to the method, although it is cost-effective compared to chlorine.
In 2007 the company launched a project for adenovirus disinfection.
In 2009 it passed a full validation at full scale with live adenovirus.
The work was led by Dr. Karl Linden of the University of Colorado at Boulder and Karl Scheible of HDR/HydroQual.
In 2013 Atlantium announced that its system had received the EPA's Environmental Technology Verification.
According to its brochure, it is the only UV system validated to this threshold with live adenovirus.
According to the brochure, in 2008 Atlantium and the Village of Mohawk were pioneers in the use of UV for 4-log virus disinfection in New York State.
In 2013 a storm flooded the village and damaged the water infrastructure.
According to the brochure, Atlantium immediately installed another unit, even before emergency funding was approved.
According to the brochure, Hillsborough, New Hampshire, also complied with the Safe Drinking Water Act a month after a company system was installed there.

stations.title: From Chennai to the Hoover Dam

paragraphs.text: According to the ATS, in Chennai, India, 1.5 million liters of lake water a day are cleaned this way and turned into drinking water.
At the Hoover Dam, according to the ATS, the technology prevents mussels from clogging the turbines.
According to the ATS, it cleans water for Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Carlsberg and Unilever.
At the Israeli pharmaceutical plant Kamada, an HOD system was installed as the primary disinfection barrier.
The HOD system for open channels received validation from Carollo Engineers.
According to the news item, it eliminates pathogens without leaving residues harmful to the environment.
The company has installations in the US, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Australia.
According to the news item, it is working with water utilities in North America and around the world to deploy the system at scale.
In December 2012 Atlantium was selected as one of six finalists in the W.E.T. Revolution competition.
32 Israeli water companies competed in the competition.
The final was set for Tel Aviv, before 150 water industry executives from the US and Israel.
Benjamin Kahn, the company's CEO in 2012, was presented as having been named a "Hero of the Environment" by Time magazine.
In 2016 the company announced that it had received American certification for contact with drinking water.
Before that, it had been certified for this under the Israeli standard.
